normalized.governing_thought: Margin fell because of promotions, e-commerce and shrink, not mainly wages; a six-lever plan gets back to ~3.0% by FY2028 within the $25M budget
executive_summary: What happened: Operating margin fell from 3.37% to 1.02% in two years (−$35M at FY2025 sales). Store labor explains just 0.30 pt of the 2.35-pt fall. Promotions (0.70), e-commerce fulfillment (0.84) and shrink (0.50) explain 2.04 pts, 87%.

Why the draft plan falls short: Cutting store hours 8% and freezing e-commerce reaches only ~1.5% margin by FY2028 even if the cut costs nothing, once the 2027 wage rise is absorbed. It also puts fresh quality at risk: stores with the fewest labor hours already run 3.1% shrink against 2.3%.

What we recommend: Fix the margin where it was lost: (1) reprice home delivery as tested; (2) cut the money-losing promotions and win back vendor funding; (3) restore receiving and produce routines to cut shrink; (4) schedule labor to demand rather than cut it across the board; (5) grow private label; (6) exit the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA, six of them as their leases expire.

What it delivers: Operating income rises from $15.3M to ~$41.5M in FY2028, about 3.0% of ~$1.40B sales, after absorbing a $6.8M wage rise. One-time cost is ~$18M of the $25M ceiling. The base case is thin (2.96%), so ~$10M of contingency levers are worked in parallel.

What to do first: Four moves in the next six months need ~$1.5M of one-time cost and add ~$7.9M a year: roll out delivery pricing, drop loss-making promotion events, reinstate receiving and rotation checks, and refuse the 3% delivery rate rise. This takes run-rate operating income to ~$23M, above the $20M covenant level.
Decisions today: Approve the plan in place of the 8% hours cut; vote on a fix-or-exit test for the three stores with leases beyond 2027; authorise the $25M envelope and a lender briefing.

normalized.recommendation: Fix the margin where it was lost: (1) reprice home delivery as tested; (2) cut the money-losing promotions and win back vendor funding; (3) restore receiving and produce routines to cut shrink; (4) schedule labor to demand rather than cut it across the board; (5) grow private label; (6) exit the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA, six of them as their leases expire. Start with four Wave 1 moves (~$1.5M, ~$7.9M a year). Board to approve the plan in place of the 8% hours cut, vote on the fix-or-exit rule for three stores, authorise the $25M envelope, and endorse delivery repricing and an early lender briefing.

alternatives_considered.option: Draft plan (CFO / COO): cut scheduled store hours 8% across the board and freeze e-commerce at its current size
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected and replaced. It addresses one source of the decline (labor, ~13%), stalls at ~$12.5M–22.5M (0.8%–1.5%) FY2028 operating income, risks +0.6–0.7 pt shrink (~$10M) with net effect ~$4.5M if shrink rises as feared; run-rate below $20M covenant if shrink rises ~$10M; freezing e-commerce locks in the ~$10M loss.
Recommended over the blanket cut: ~$5.1M net labor saving, shrink −0.3 pt (+$4.2M), net effect ~$9.3M, low customer risk.
Delivery is kept 'as the owners want', at tested prices with click-and-collect as default; the remaining ~$7.6M a year loss is 'the visible cost of that choice'.

alternatives_considered.option: Second delivery pricing step (e.g. delivery membership or higher minimum basket)
alternatives_considered.treatment: To be tested before committing it.

alternatives_considered.option: Three stores with leases beyond 2027: exit vs fix
alternatives_considered.treatment: Run for two quarters on the full plan; exit any still negative at the Q3 FY2027 review (board vote).

assumptions_and_uncertainties: The base case is thin (2.96%), within ~$0.5M of the target, so there is no slack; ~$10M of contingency levers are worked in parallel.
The ~$10M shrink estimate for an 8% cut is an association, not a measured effect.
The comparable-sales comparison (+1.8% vs +0.2%) does not control for store differences and is treated as a correlation.
E-commerce incremental view: 30% of e-commerce sales genuinely new × 20¢ contribution per new dollar (finance estimate); in-store-diverted sales add no contribution.
Delivery test results (4 stores, 10 weeks) are assumed to scale chain-wide.
Promotion sizing assumes 30% of the margin recovered is given back in lost volume.
Vendor funding assumes the 14-pt promotional margin gap is net of funding (~$113M markdowns); if gross, the lever needs re-sizing.
Private label pace of ~1 pt a year is assumed achievable (vs 0.75 pt historically).
Chain is assumed able to reach the Q4 shrink level of 2.3%.
Net 3% labor hours reduction assumed achievable without service loss.
Split of nine stores between six and three assumed pro rata; closure cost for the six (~$0.5M a store) is a planning allowance.
At least 25% of closed stores' sales assumed to transfer to nearby Harlow stores.
Wage line assumes the 4% minimum-wage rise flows through the entire store pay scale (conservative); only this step is modelled, other inflation assumed passed through prices.
Only the $7.5M lease-exit cost is from the pack; other one-time costs are planning allowances to be validated by finance.
No FY2026 actuals in the pack; covenant tested on run-rate after Wave 1.
Delivery contract renews in 2026 and may already be signed at +3%.
FY2025 taken as February 2025 to January 2026.
Main risks: ValuMart response to fewer promotions, vendor resistance, scheduling hurting service, delivery customers leaving, larger wage rise, fewer sales following closed stores.
